name: J&M Recording Studio
writeup: Cosimo Matassa was still a teenager when he put recording gear in a back room of his family's J&M Music Shop at North Rampart and Dumaine streets. The room measured about fifteen by sixteen feet, yet from the mid-1940s until Matassa moved to Governor Nicholls Street in 1956 it captured the sound that became rock and roll: Roy Brown's "Good Rocking Tonight" (1947), Fats Domino's "The Fat Man" (1949), Professor Longhair's "Tipitina" (1953) and Little Richard's "Tutti Frutti" (1955). The building, long a laundromat, still stands on the edge of the French Quarter.

name: Dew Drop Inn
writeup: Barber Frank Painia opened the Dew Drop Inn at 2836 LaSalle Street in 1939 and added a nightclub in 1945. In segregated New Orleans it gave Black entertainers both a stage and a respectable place to sleep. Its floor shows drew Ray Charles, Big Joe Turner, Guitar Slim, Earl King, Allen Toussaint, Dave Bartholomew and James Booker, and Little Richard sang about the place. The music room went quiet around 1970 and Painia died in 1972. After decades of decline the building was restored and reopened in 2024 as a hotel and music venue.

name: Blue Room, Roosevelt Hotel
writeup: The Blue Room opened in the Roosevelt Hotel in 1935 and for decades was the city's premier supper club. Touring big bands led by Glenn Miller, Tommy Dorsey and Guy Lombardo played here, followed by singers such as Lena Horne, Sarah Vaughan, Frank Sinatra and Tony Bennett. Radio station WWL carried live broadcasts of the dance bands, so the room's sound reached listeners far beyond the hotel. It stopped operating as a supper club in 1989, closed after Hurricane Katrina in 2005, and returned when the restored Roosevelt reopened in 2009.

name: Preservation Hall
writeup: In the 1950s Larry Borenstein let older jazz musicians hold informal sessions in his art gallery at 726 St. Peter Street. In 1961 Allan and Sandra Jaffe took over and turned the worn early-1800s building into Preservation Hall, a plain room with benches, no bar and no air conditioning, devoted to traditional New Orleans jazz. Players such as Sweet Emma Barrett, George Lewis, Punch Miller, and Billie and De De Pierce found steady work and new audiences there. Under Jim Crow it was a rare place where integrated bands and audiences shared a room. The touring Preservation Hall Jazz Band grew out of it.

name: Fats Domino's House
writeup: Antoine "Fats" Domino was born in New Orleans in 1928 and grew up in the Lower Ninth Ward. Even after his piano-driven records made him a star of early rock and roll, he preferred to stay in the old neighborhood, building a home at 1208 Caffin Avenue in the 1960s. The house became a neighborhood landmark and a sign of what a Black artist could achieve in the segregated South. Domino was rescued from it by boat during the flooding that followed Hurricane Katrina in 2005. He died in 2017. The restored house is closed to the public, and its street now also carries his name.

name: Louisiana State Penitentiary at Angola
writeup: In the summer of 1933 folklorist John Lomax and his son Alan brought a recording machine to the state prison farm at Angola, collecting African American songs for the Library of Congress. The warden pointed them to a prisoner named Huddie Ledbetter, known as Lead Belly. They returned in July 1934 with better equipment and recorded him again, including "Irene," the song later famous as "Goodnight Irene," "The Midnight Special," and a plea addressed to Governor O.K. Allen. Lead Belly was released that August and went on to national fame. The sessions made Angola a landmark in the documentation of American folk music.

name: Temple Roof Garden (Prince Hall Masonic Temple)
writeup: Built in 1924 for the Grand United Order of Odd Fellows, the four-story building at 1335 North Boulevard held the Temple Theatre and, on its top floor, a ballroom called the Temple Roof Garden. With no comparable hall open to them, Black Baton Rougeans and students from Southern University danced here to touring bands; people interviewed for the building's National Register nomination recalled Fats Waller, Duke Ellington, Louis Armstrong and Cab Calloway. A 1938 advertisement called it the finest dancing hall in the South. The Prince Hall Masons bought the building in 1948, and it was listed on the National Register in 1994.

name: Slim Harpo Marker and Mulatto Bend Cemetery
writeup: James Moore, who recorded as Slim Harpo, was born in February 1924 at Lobdell in West Baton Rouge Parish. He worked as a longshoreman and construction laborer and played Baton Rouge bars before his recording career began in 1957 with "I'm a King Bee." "Rainin' in My Heart" (1961) and "Baby Scratch My Back" (1966) both reached the top five of the rhythm and blues chart, and the Rolling Stones, the Kinks and many others recorded his songs. He died in 1970 at age 46 and is buried beside his parents in Mulatto Bend Cemetery. A state historical marker stands at U.S. 190 and South Mulatto Bend Road.

name: Buddy Guy Birthplace
writeup: George "Buddy" Guy was born on July 30, 1936, in Lettsworth, a rural community in northern Pointe Coupee Parish, the son of a sharecropper. He absorbed the sounds of Louisiana players and of Mississippi bluesmen such as Muddy Waters and B.B. King, and in 1957 left Baton Rouge for Chicago, where he became a giant of electric blues guitar. A Mississippi Blues Trail marker was unveiled on December 8, 2018, beside Louisiana Highway 418 at Sharkles Place; its text says the family's house stood a short distance away. The highway through Lettsworth is now named Buddy Guy Way.
sources: OffBeat Magazine: Buddy Guy Mississippi Blues Trail marker <https://offbeat.com/news/buddy-guy-mississippi-blues-trail> | Historical Marker Database: Buddy Guy <https://www.hmdb.org/m.asp?m=127700>

name: Haney's Big House
writeup: William Haney, a World War I veteran and Black businessman, turned a 1930s barbecue stand in Ferriday into Haney's Big House, a nightclub with a dance floor, a motel for performers and even a bus ticket counter. At its peak from 1940 to 1966 it was a stop on the Chitlin' Circuit, hosting Ray Charles, B.B. King, Big Joe Turner, Roy Brown and Irma Thomas. A young Jerry Lee Lewis and his cousin Jimmy Swaggart listened from the sidewalk, then tried the music at the piano. The club burned in 1966 and was not rebuilt. A Blues Trail marker at North First and Greathouse streets tells the story.

name: Miller-Roy Building and Savoy Ballroom
writeup: Two Black physicians, J.T. Miller and J.C. Roy, built this three-story block at DeSiard and Tenth streets in 1929 as a home for African American business in segregated Monroe. Offices, a pharmacy and a newspaper filled the lower floors, and the third floor was the Savoy Ballroom, a Chitlin' Circuit stop that brought Louis Armstrong, Lena Horne, Billie Holiday and later Otis Redding and Percy Sledge to northeast Louisiana. The building was eventually condemned and approved for demolition, but it was listed on the National Register in 2011 and has since been renovated as apartments with community space.
sources: 64 Parishes: Monroe's Miller-Roy Building <https://64parishes.org/monroes-miller-roy-building>

name: Calanthean Temple
writeup: The Grand Court Order of Calanthe, a Black women's fraternal organization led by Cora Murdock Allen, completed this four-story building on Texas Avenue in 1923. It held offices for Black doctors, dentists and lawyers, and its rooftop garden became a leading dance spot for African Americans in Jim Crow Shreveport. Duke Ellington, Louis Armstrong, Jelly Roll Morton, Cab Calloway and Louis Jordan are among those reported to have played there, and touring musicians came up for late jam sessions after their engagements at segregated venues. The roof garden's heyday was the 1930s and 1940s. The long-neglected building is now part of the Shreveport Common revitalization effort.
sources: 64 Parishes: Music in the Court of Calanthe <https://64parishes.org/music-in-the-court-of-calanthe> | Downtown Shreveport: Calanthean Temple, rooftop dances and legendary musicians <https://downtownshreveport.com/featured/calanthean-temple-rooftop-dances-and-legendary-musicians/>

name: Shreveport Municipal Auditorium (Louisiana Hayride)
writeup: From April 1948 until 1960 the Art Deco Municipal Auditorium was home to the Louisiana Hayride, a Saturday night barn dance sent out over Shreveport's 50,000-watt station KWKH. The show earned the nickname "Cradle of the Stars" because so many performers rose from its stage to national fame: Hank Williams first, then Webb Pierce, Slim Whitman, Jim Reeves, Johnny Cash, Johnny Horton and, beginning in 1954, a young Elvis Presley, whose mix of country, gospel and rhythm and blues pointed toward rock and roll. The building, constructed between 1926 and 1929, was named a National Historic Landmark in 2008.

name: Goldband Records
writeup: Eddie Shuler, a Texas-born guitarist who came to Lake Charles in the early 1940s, started Goldband in 1945 to record his own band and soon turned to the musicians around him. The complex on Church Street held a studio, production rooms and a record shop. Its catalog ran from Iry LeJeune's Cajun accordion to Boozoo Chavis's "Paper in My Shoe" (1954), Phil Phillips's swamp pop hit "Sea of Love" (1959) and the first record by a thirteen-year-old Dolly Parton. When Shuler died in 2005 Goldband was described as the country's longest-established independent label. The complex was demolished in 2017; a historical marker stands on Church Street.

name: J.D. Miller Recording Studio (museum at Crowley City Hall)
writeup: J.D. Miller set up his first simple recording room in Crowley in 1947 and went on to record nearly every style heard in south Louisiana: Cajun, country, zydeco, swamp pop and, above all, swamp blues. From 1957 he licensed sides by Lightnin' Slim, Slim Harpo and others to Excello Records, giving the rest of the country its idea of the Louisiana blues sound. The legacy is mixed, since in the 1960s Miller also issued openly racist records. His MasterTrak studio, built in 1967, later hosted John Fogerty and Paul Simon. A museum of his studio equipment is inside Crowley City Hall, which is the point mapped here.

name: Floyd's Record Shop (Swallow and Jin Records)
writeup: Floyd Soileau began selling records in 1956 from a small room at radio station KVPI, where he hosted a Cajun music show, and by 1958 had launched two labels: Swallow for Cajun music and Jin for the rock-and-roll-flavored style later called swamp pop. Jin scored with Rod Bernard's "This Should Go On Forever," Joe Barry's "I'm a Fool to Care" and Tommy McLain's "Sweet Dreams," while Swallow's 1965 Balfa Brothers album helped spark the Cajun revival. The longtime East Main Street store closed in 2012; a smaller shop reopened in 2016 on South Chataignier Street, which is the point mapped here.

name: Fred's Lounge
writeup: Alfred "Fred" Tate bought a bar on Mamou's Sixth Street on November 20, 1946, and it became a small-town headquarters for the Cajun revival. Tate and his friends Revon Reed and Paul Tate used it to help bring back Mamou's Courir de Mardi Gras, and in 1962 Reed started a live Saturday morning radio show from the lounge, broadcast in Louisiana French over KVPI in Ville Platte. The show has continued ever since. After Fred died in 1992, Sue Vasseur, known as Tante Sue, kept the lounge going. It opens only on Saturday mornings for most of the year, with a Cajun band and dancing from nine o'clock.

name: Slim's Y-Ki-Ki
writeup: Arnold "Slim" Gradney and his wife Irene Pratt Gradney ran this dance hall on the highway north of Opelousas, one of the first clubs where zydeco took shape. The usual founding date is 1947, although license records suggest the Y-Ki-Ki name, a nod to Slim's interest in Hawaii, was adopted around 1960. Clifton Chenier, John Delafose, Rockin' Sidney, Beau Jocque and later Keith Frank filled the floor with dancers. The Gradneys' son Tony closed the club in 2016, citing rising band fees and unruly crowds. A local zydeco preservation society has since been working toward restoring the building.

name: Richard's Club
writeup: Eddie Richard opened this wooden roadhouse on U.S. 190 in Lawtell in 1947. In the 1950s it booked touring rhythm and blues acts such as B.B. King, Big Joe Turner and Jimmy Reed. After Richard began hiring Clifton Chenier it became the best-known zydeco dance hall anywhere, nicknamed the Grand Ole Opry of zydeco. Boozoo Chavis recorded a comeback album there in 1989, and John Delafose suffered a fatal heart attack on its stage in 1994. Eddie's son Kermon ran it from 1979 until his death in 2004. It closed as Richard's in 2006, later reopened as Miller's Zydeco Hall of Fame, and burned in 2017.
sources: OffBeat Magazine: Zydeco's Grand Ole Opry <https://www.offbeat.com/articles/zydecos-grand-ole-opry> | Wikipedia: Richard's Club <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard%27s_Club>

name: La Poussière
writeup: La Poussière, French for "the dust," is a Cajun dance hall that the Patin family opened in Breaux Bridge in 1955. When the highway department took the original site for a right-of-way, the club moved across the road to the red brick building it occupies today. Lawrence Patin, who started managing it at eighteen, has kept it going for more than half a century. Long devoted to Cajun bands alone, it has recently added zydeco, and it remains one of the few old Louisiana dance halls still standing, with live music every weekend.
